title: Parables of the Kingdom
summary: Teaching from a boat, Jesus tells the parable of the sower and explains to his disciples why he speaks in parables, quoting Isaiah 6:9-10. He adds parables of weeds among wheat, a mustard seed, leaven, hidden treasure, a pearl, and a dragnet, explains the sower and the weeds, and ends with a saying about the scribe trained for the kingdom. Returning to Nazareth, he is rejected by his own town and does few miracles there because of their unbelief.
story:
Chapters 11 and 12 showed Jesus meeting doubt from John in prison, indifference from the towns where he had worked, and open hostility from Pharisees who said he cast out demons by Beelzebul. They closed with Jesus naming as his mother and brothers whoever does the will of his Father (12:50). Chapter 13 explains that division. If the kingdom of heaven has arrived, why do so many refuse it, and why does it look so small? The parables answer: the message is like seed that falls on different kinds of ground; the kingdom begins small and hidden and grows; good and evil will grow side by side until the end, when God alone will separate them; and those who see its worth give up everything for it with joy.

This is the third of Matthew's five great discourses, standing at the center of the Gospel, and it closes with the formula “When Jesus had finished these parables” (13:53), as the others do. The chapter then turns to Nazareth, where the people who know Jesus best take offense at him, a living example of the hard ground the parables describe. From here the Gospel moves into a section in which Jesus withdraws more often and gives more time to his disciples, until Peter confesses him as the Christ in chapter 16.
historical:
The phrase kingdom of heaven, which introduces almost every parable here, occurs 32 times in Matthew and nowhere else in the New Testament; Matthew uses kingdom of God only a handful of times (12:28, 19:24, 21:31, 21:43). Mark and Luke say kingdom of God in the parallel passages, so the two phrases name the same thing: God's reign, not a place in the sky. The older explanation is that Matthew, writing for Jewish Christians, followed the custom of avoiding God's name out of reverence, as later rabbinic usage often did. Jonathan Pennington (Heaven and Earth in the Gospel of Matthew, 2007) argued that this is not the whole story: Matthew uses heaven deliberately, pairing it with earth throughout his Gospel, to set God's realm against the present order of the world and to look for the day when his will is done on earth as in heaven (6:10).

Many Jews of the Second Temple period expected God's reign to come all at once and in power. Daniel had seen a kingdom that God would set up to crush the empires and never be destroyed (Daniel 2:44), and the Psalms of Solomon, written in the first century BC after Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, prayed for a son of David who would purge Jerusalem of Gentiles and gather a holy people (Psalms of Solomon 17:21-32). The War Scroll from Qumran (1QM) pictured a final battle of the sons of light against the sons of darkness. Against these hopes the parables describe something unexpected: a kingdom already present in Jesus but hidden, small, resisted, and mixed with evil, whose full arrival and judgment still lie ahead.

The parable of the sower has parallels in Mark 4:1-20 and Luke 8:4-15; the mustard seed in Mark 4:30-32 and Luke 13:18-19; the leaven in Luke 13:20-21. The weeds, the treasure, the pearl, the dragnet, and the scribe are found only in Matthew. The Gospel of Thomas, a collection of sayings found in Coptic at Nag Hammadi in Egypt in 1945 (with Greek fragments from Oxyrhynchus), has its own forms of the sower (saying 9), the mustard seed (20), the weeds (57), the pearl (76), the leaven (96), the treasure (109), and a wise fisherman who keeps one large fish from his net (8); its date and its relation to the canonical Gospels are debated.

Buried treasure was a real feature of the ancient economy. In a land crossed by armies and without banks, families hid coins and valuables in the ground, and when the owner died or fled the hoard could lie forgotten. Josephus says that after the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 the Romans dug up much of the gold, silver, and other valuables the Jews had buried against the uncertainties of war, and captives pointed out still more (Jewish War 7.114-115). The Copper Scroll from Qumran Cave 3 (3Q15), found in 1952 and engraved on copper, lists dozens of places where treasure was said to be hidden. The rejection at Nazareth is told also in Mark 6:1-6, and Luke 4:16-30 gives a fuller account set at the start of the ministry. Nazareth was a small village in the hills of lower Galilee, about four miles from Sepphoris, which Herod Antipas rebuilt as his capital during Jesus' youth (Josephus, Antiquities 18.27).
cultural:
Every image in the chapter comes from ordinary Galilean life. Farmers scattered seed by hand, and some fell on paths packed hard by feet, on thin soil over limestone, and among thorn roots (see the note on Mark 4 for the debate over whether sowing came before plowing). A yield of thirty, sixty, or a hundredfold would have sounded remarkable; Isaac's hundredfold in Genesis 26:12 is a mark of the Lord's blessing. The weed of verse 25 (zizanion) is usually identified as darnel (Lolium temulentum), a grass that looks almost exactly like wheat until it heads and whose grain, often infected by a fungus, causes dizziness and nausea if eaten. The Mishnah names it (zunin) and rules that wheat and darnel are not diverse kinds for the law of mixed sowing, a sign of how closely they were thought to resemble each other (m. Kilayim 1:1). Sowing darnel in an enemy's field was a real act of malice: the Roman jurist Ulpian, quoting the older lawyer Celsus, discusses the legal remedy against a man who sowed darnel in another's crop to spoil it (Digest 9.2.27.14).

The mustard was probably black mustard (Brassica nigra), which grows around the lake to two or three meters in a season. Its seed was proverbially tiny: the Mishnah uses a mustard seed as the measure of the smallest amount (m. Niddah 5:2). Leaven was a lump of fermented dough kept from the last baking; in Scripture it can picture corruption (16:6, 1 Corinthians 5:6-8), but here it pictures hidden, pervasive growth. Three measures (sata, from the Hebrew seah) came to about an ephah, well over twenty liters of flour, the amount Sarah baked for her three guests (Genesis 18:6), bread for a crowd.

Pearls stood at the top of the ancient scale of value. Pliny the Elder, writing in the 70s AD, says that pearls hold the first place among all precious things (Natural History 9.106) and tells how Cleopatra dissolved one of a famous pair in vinegar to win a wager (9.119-121). They came from the Red Sea, the Persian Gulf, and India, and a merchant (emporos) dealing in them was a wholesale trader who traveled, not a village shopkeeper. The dragnet (sagēnē) was a long weighted net drawn through the water from a boat or hauled to shore, catching everything in its path; fish without fins and scales were unclean under Leviticus 11:9-12 and would be thrown away.

The smallest of all seeds raises a question a modern reader will notice, since orchid seeds, for example, are far smaller than mustard. The strongest form of the objection is that Jesus, or Matthew, states as fact something botanically false. The philosopher Stephen T. Davis (The Debate about the Bible, 1977) counted the saying as one of the Bible's minor errors, arguing that Scripture is infallible in matters of faith and practice but not in every detail. Defenders of inerrancy have answered in two ways. Harold Lindsell (The Battle for the Bible, 1976) held that the speaker meant the smallest seed his hearers were accustomed to sow, and John A. Sproule (Grace Theological Journal, 1980) argued that seed in an agricultural saying means seed sown in field and garden, among which mustard was indeed the least. The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978, Article XIII) states the principle both answers share, that observational descriptions of nature and the lack of modern technical precision do not count against Scripture's truthfulness. Readers across these positions agree on what the parable is doing: using the proverbial smallest thing that Galileans knew to picture a kingdom whose beginnings looked negligible.

At Nazareth the townspeople know the family. Jesus is the son of a tektōn, a builder or craftsman in wood or stone, and they name his mother and four brothers and mention his sisters. The proverb of verse 57 circulated widely: it appears in John 4:44 and in the Gospel of Thomas (saying 31), where it is paired with the saying that a doctor does not heal those who know him.
literary:
A parable (parabolē) is a comparison drawn from life that invites the hearer to see something familiar in a new light. The Hebrew counterpart, mashal, covers proverbs, riddles, taunts, and extended stories, and the Greek Old Testament translates it with parabolē. Matthew builds the chapter with care. The first half is spoken to the crowds by the sea (verses 1 to 35), and the second to the disciples in the house (verses 36 to 52); the move indoors at verse 36 marks the turn from public riddles to private instruction. Many commentators count seven parables, a number that suits Matthew's fondness for grouping: the sower, the weeds, the mustard seed, the leaven, the treasure, the pearl, and the net, followed by the saying about the scribe, which Matthew also calls a comparison. The parables come in pairs and in frames. The sower and the weeds each receive a full explanation. The mustard seed and the leaven, a man in a field and a woman at home, make one point about small beginnings and a great end. The treasure and the pearl, one found by accident and one found by searching, make one point about joyful sacrifice for supreme worth. The weeds and the net both end at the close of the age with a separation carried out by angels, and they share the refrain of the furnace and the weeping and gnashing of teeth (verses 42 and 50).

The chapter keeps returning to hearing and understanding. The verb akouō, to hear, occurs sixteen times, and suniēmi, to understand, six; the refrain “He who has ears, let him hear” frames the public teaching (verses 9 and 43); the good soil is the one who hears and understands (verse 23), in contrast to the one who hears and does not understand (verse 19). The disciples' answer to Jesus' question “Have you understood all these things?” (verse 51) is a plain yes, a notable change from Mark, where the disciples' understanding is regularly in doubt (Mark 4:13). Matthew also presents Jesus' parable-speaking as fulfilled prophecy (verses 14 and 35), with two formal quotations where Mark has an allusion.

Since Adolf Jülicher (Die Gleichnisreden Jesu, 1888 and 1899) scholars have debated whether a parable makes one main point or can carry several points of comparison. The explanations Jesus gives here show that some parables at least carry allegorical detail (the field, the enemy, the harvesters), while the short paired parables make a single comparison. The saying about the scribe in verse 52 closes the discourse by turning from the kingdom to the teacher who has been formed by it, and many readers have heard in it Matthew's description of his own work, a Gospel that brings out of the storeroom of Israel's Scripture both old treasures and new.

doctrines.note: The chapter teaches that God's reign is already present in Jesus but hidden and growing, mixed with evil in the world until the end of the age, when it will be revealed and the wicked separated from the righteous. Theologians often call this the already and the not yet: begun in Jesus' ministry, completed at his return (verses 40 to 43).

“The knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven has been given to you” (verse 11): understanding is a gift, not a discovery. Parables open to those who come to Jesus and ask, as the disciples do in verses 10 and 36, and remain closed to those who will not, and the chapter presents Jesus as the one who utters “things hidden since the foundation of the world” (verse 35).

Verses 11 to 15 apply Isaiah's commission to Jesus' parables: God gives understanding to some and leaves others in the blindness they have chosen. Matthew's “because” (verse 13) stresses the hearers' own closed eyes (verse 15), while verse 11 stresses God's giving. Christians have weighed the two differently (see the first hard question).

Jesus says “The field is the world” (verse 38), but from Augustine to Calvin (Institutes 4.1.13) the parables of the weeds and the net have been read as a picture of the visible church as a mixed body until the end, against movements that sought a church of the pure. The servants are forbidden to uproot the weeds; the separation belongs to the Son of Man's angels at the harvest.

The weeds and the net both end in a separation at the end of the age, carried out by angels at the Son of Man's command, with fire for the wicked and glory for the righteous, who “will shine like the sun” (verse 43, echoing Daniel 12:3). Final judgment belongs to God, not to his servants, and its delay is patience, not indifference.

words.note: Parabolē, parable. It occurs about 50 times in the New Testament: 17 in Matthew, 13 in Mark, 18 in Luke, and twice in Hebrews (9:9, 11:19), where it means a figure or type. Twelve of Matthew's uses are in this chapter. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the Hebrew mashal, and BDAG describes its range in the Gospels as running from a full narrative to a short figurative saying or riddle. In verse 13 Jesus gives it as his chosen mode of speech to the crowds, and in verse 34 Matthew says he spoke to them in nothing else.

Mystērion, mystery or secret. It occurs 28 times in the New Testament but only once in each Synoptic Gospel (here, Mark 4:11, Luke 8:10); Paul uses it most. It came into biblical Greek in Daniel 2, where it renders the Aramaic raz, a secret of God's purposes that only God reveals (Daniel 2:28), and the Dead Sea Scrolls use raz in the same way. Matthew, like Luke, has the plural, the mysteries of the kingdom: not puzzles for the clever but truths about God's reign, once hidden and now given (verse 11).

Zizanion, weeds, the darnel that resembles wheat. It occurs eight times in the New Testament, all in this chapter (verses 25 to 40), and nowhere in the Greek Old Testament. The English tares comes from older translations (Tyndale and the King James Version). The word's meaning is the point of the parable: in the present age the sons of the kingdom and the sons of the evil one can look alike, and an attempt to root one out would damage the other (verse 29).

Sunteleia, completion or consummation. It occurs six times in the New Testament: five in Matthew, always in the phrase the end of the age (13:39, 40, 49; 24:3; 28:20), and once in Hebrews 9:26 of Christ's appearing at the culmination of the ages. The Greek versions of Daniel use it for the time of the end (Daniel 12:4). In Matthew it marks history as moving to a goal set by God, and the same phrase closes the Gospel with Jesus' promise to be with his disciples until then.

Thēsauros, treasure, and also the chest or storeroom that holds it. It occurs 17 times in the New Testament, nine in Matthew: the Magi's treasure chests (2:11), treasure in heaven (6:19-21, 19:21), the good and evil treasure of the heart (12:35), the hidden treasure (13:44), and the storeroom of the scribe (13:52). BDAG gives both senses, and verse 52 plays on them. Paul says all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ (Colossians 2:3).

Margaritēs, pearl. It occurs nine times in the New Testament: in Jesus' warning not to throw pearls before pigs (7:6), in this parable (13:45-46), as a sign of luxury (1 Timothy 2:9; Revelation 17:4, 18:12, 18:16), and in the twelve gates of the new Jerusalem, each made of a single pearl (Revelation 21:21). In the ancient world it was the costliest of gems, and the merchant's single pearl is worth everything he owns.

Mathēteuō, to make a disciple or to be discipled. It occurs only four times in the New Testament: here (verse 52), of Joseph of Arimathea, who ‘had become a disciple’ of Jesus (27:57), in the Great Commission, ‘make disciples of all nations’ (28:19), and in Acts 14:21. In verse 52 the aorist passive participle describes a scribe who has been trained or made a disciple for (or in) the kingdom. Three of its four uses are Matthew's, and they tie the chapter to the Gospel's last command.

Adelphos, brother. It occurs about 343 times in the New Testament. Its first sense is a son of the same parents, but in the Bible it also covers wider kin, as when Abram calls his nephew Lot his brother (Genesis 13:8, where the Greek Old Testament uses adelphos), and it becomes Jesus' word for his disciples (12:49-50, 23:8, 28:10). In verse 55 it names James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas, and how far its range reaches here is the heart of a long debate among Christians (see the second hard question).

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus as both the teller and the subject of the parables. In the explanation of the weeds, the Son of Man sows the good seed, owns the field, sends the angels, and has a kingdom of his own (verses 37 and 41), and the righteous shine in the kingdom of their Father (verse 43). The one speaking in riddles by the lake is the judge of the end of the age. Matthew twice presents his parable-speaking as fulfillment. The words of Isaiah 6, spoken first of Isaiah's ministry to a people who would not hear, find their fullest instance in the reception of Jesus (verses 14 and 15), and Psalm 78:2, where Asaph, whom 2 Chronicles 29:30 calls a seer, opens his mouth in a parable to tell Israel's history as a lesson, is applied to Jesus, who utters “things hidden since the foundation of the world” (verse 35). The link with the psalm is a pattern rather than a prediction: the psalmist drew hidden lessons out of Israel's past, and Jesus reveals what God had hidden from the beginning.

Verse 17 states the chapter's claim most directly: “many prophets and righteous men longed to see what you see but did not see it.” The disciples are standing where Israel's hopes are being met, and what they see is Jesus himself. The mustard seed that becomes a tree where the birds of the air nest echoes the great trees of Ezekiel 17:23 and Daniel 4:12, pictures of kingdoms that shelter the nations; Ezekiel's is a sprig God himself plants on the mountain of Israel. The echo suggests that the small beginning in Galilee will become the refuge the prophets foresaw, including for the Gentiles.

The treasure and the pearl speak of the kingdom rather than naming Jesus, but the church has long read them of him, since the kingdom comes in his person. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.26.1) said Christ is the treasure hidden in the field of the Scriptures, pointed out by types and parables and brought to light by the cross. The scribe of verse 52, who brings new and old out of his storeroom, describes the way Matthew reads Israel's Scriptures in the light of Christ. And at Nazareth the one who teaches the mysteries of heaven is dismissed as the carpenter's son. His neighbors' offense is a first taste of the rejection that will end at the cross, where the kingdom will be revealed in the most hidden form of all.
interpretation:
Jewish readers have long recognized the parables as belonging to their own tradition of meshalim. The rabbis told parables of kings, fields, and treasure; the Mekhilta of Rabbi Ishmael, commenting on Pharaoh's regret in Exodus 14:5, compares Egypt to a man who sold cheaply a field he had inherited and then watched the buyer find treasure in it. The Babylonian Talmud tells of a Gentile who sold all his property and bought a pearl, only for it to be found in a fish bought by Joseph who honored the Sabbath (b. Shabbat 119a). David Flusser and Amy-Jill Levine (Short Stories by Jesus, 2014, with chapters on the mustard seed, the leaven, and the pearl) have read Jesus' parables as the work of a Jewish teacher and warned against readings that make them attacks on Judaism.

The church fathers read the chapter christologically and morally. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.26.1) made the hidden treasure Christ concealed in the Scriptures. Origen's Commentary on Matthew, book 10 (the 240s), made the field the Scripture and the treasure the hidden sense beneath its letter, and the scribe of verse 52 the teacher who dispenses both the literal and the spiritual sense. John Chrysostom (Homily 45 on Matthew, around 390) insisted that verse 13 places the blame on the hearers, whose blindness was self-chosen. Jerome (Against Jovinian 1.3) matched the hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold to virgins, widows, and the married, a reading later interpreters rejected.

The weeds among the wheat have had a remarkable history in debates over the church and over toleration. In the Donatist controversy in North Africa, the Donatists claimed to be a pure church and argued that the field is the world, not the church; Augustine answered that the church spread through the world is itself the field in which wheat and weeds grow until the harvest, a mixed body (corpus permixtum), and he pressed the point at the Conference of Carthage in 411. Yet Augustine also came to defend imperial coercion of the Donatists, reading ‘compel them to come in’ (Luke 14:23) in that light (Letter 93, 408), though he pleaded against executing them. Chrysostom (Homily 46 on Matthew) read verse 29 as forbidding the killing of heretics while allowing them to be silenced. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II q.11 a.3) cited the same verse and answered that it forbids uprooting only where the wheat would be harmed, so that heretics may justly be put to death.

At the Reformation the parable became a charter for toleration. Balthasar Hubmaier's Concerning Heretics and Those Who Burn Them (1524) built on it, and Luther's sermon on the text in his Church Postil (1525) argued that heretics must not be burned, since one who goes astray today may find the right way tomorrow. Luther later signed Philip Melanchthon's memorandum of 1536 allowing the death penalty for Anabaptists as seditious, a reversal his critics have never let pass. Calvin (Institutes 4.1.13) used the weeds and the net against Anabaptists who sought a church of the perfect. In New England, Roger Williams argued in The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution (1644) that because the field is the world, the magistrate must leave dissenters and unbelievers alone until the harvest; John Cotton replied (The Bloudy Tenent, Washed, 1647) that the field is the church. Williams's reading helped shape the American tradition of religious liberty.

Modern study runs from Jülicher's single-point rule through C. H. Dodd (The Parables of the Kingdom, 1935) and Joachim Jeremias (The Parables of Jesus, 1947), who read the mustard seed and leaven as parables of contrast, to Jack Dean Kingsbury (The Parables of Jesus in Matthew 13, 1969), who read the chapter as Matthew's address to his own church, and David Orton (The Understanding Scribe, 1989), who read verse 52 against the ideal scribe of Jewish tradition. The Scofield Reference Bible (1909) read the chapter as the mystery form of the kingdom in the church age, with the birds and the leaven as evil, a reading most commentators reject. The Revised Common Lectionary reads the chapter in Year A (Propers 10 to 12), the Roman lectionary on the Fifteenth to Seventeenth Sundays in Ordinary Time, and the historic Western lectionary read the weeds on the Fifth Sunday after Epiphany. Henry Alford's harvest hymn Come, Ye Thankful People, Come (1844) makes the world God's field where wheat and tares are sown together, and John Everett Millais's engravings for The Parables of Our Lord (1864) include the enemy sowing tares by night.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from manuscripts. In verse 35 the earliest witnesses read simply “the prophet”, but the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and a few other witnesses read ‘Isaiah the prophet’. Jerome knew the reading and reported that the pagan critic Porphyry used it to charge Matthew with error, since the words come from Psalm 78:2; Jerome suggested that the original read Asaph and that copyists substituted a better-known name. Nearly all editors judge ‘Isaiah’ a scribal slip, perhaps prompted by Matthew's other quotations from Isaiah (8:17, 12:17). In the same verse ‘of the world’ is missing from Codex Vaticanus and others, and the Nestle-Aland text prints it in brackets. In verse 55 the critical texts read Joseph as the name of the second brother, while the later manuscripts behind the King James Version read Joses, the form found in Mark 6:3. In verses 9 and 43 later manuscripts have the fuller ‘ears to hear’, as in the King James Version, where the earliest have simply “ears”.

The quotation in verses 14 and 15 follows the Greek Old Testament of Isaiah 6:9-10 word for word, including the future ‘I will heal them’ after ‘otherwise’, where the Hebrew is more pointed; the same Greek form appears in Acts 28:26-27, while John 12:40 quotes the passage differently. Translation choices a reader will notice include ‘tares’ (KJV) for ‘weeds’, ‘leaven’ or ‘yeast’ in verse 33, and ‘three measures’ against modern conversions such as ‘sixty pounds’. Verse 32's lachanon is ‘herbs’ in the KJV and ‘garden plants’ in modern versions. In verse 52 the scribe is ‘instructed unto the kingdom’ (KJV), ‘trained for the kingdom’ (ESV), or “discipled in the kingdom” (BSB), because the Greek dative can express either the sphere or the goal of the training.

teach.big: The kingdom of heaven has come in Jesus in a hidden, small, and resisted form, so that everything depends on how one hears him, and those who understand its worth give up everything for it with joy while leaving the final sorting to God.

outline.t: The same word falls on every kind of hearer; what differs is the ground, and the harvest in good soil outruns every loss.
Understanding is a gift given to those who come to Jesus and ask, and to refuse the light is to lose even what one had.
Shallow joy, trouble, worry, and wealth each choke the word in their own way; true hearing understands and bears fruit.
Evil in the world is an enemy's work, not the owner's, and the servants' zeal to uproot it must yield to the owner's patience.
God's reign begins too small to notice and ends by filling everything, so small beginnings are no measure of its future.
Jesus' parables are themselves revelation, bringing out what God had hidden since creation.
The Son of Man will separate good and evil at the end; until then the righteous live among the weeds and wait to shine.
Whether found by surprise or after long searching, the kingdom is worth everything, and the one who finds it gives up all things in joy, not grief.
The net gathers every kind now; the sorting is sure, it is God's, and it waits for the end of the age.
Disciples who understand become teachers who bring out both the old treasures of Scripture and the new light Jesus sheds on them.
Familiarity can breed offense: those who think they know Jesus best may receive least from him.

teach.pitfalls:
The sower is often preached as a lesson in soil improvement, leaving hearers anxious to classify themselves or others. The parable's first word is about the sower's extravagance and the harvest's size, and its explanation describes kinds of hearing to be warned by, not labels to pin on people. Teachers should also resist making the hundred, sixty, and thirty into ranks of Christians, as Jerome did.

The weeds among the wheat has been misused in two opposite ways. It has been cited to justify burning heretics (Aquinas's reading) and, in a softer form, to excuse a church that never exercises discipline. The first ignores the owner's plain command; the second forgets that Matthew 18:15-20 gives the church a real, if limited, discipline and that the parable itself says the field is the world. Its point is that final judgment belongs to God, not that sin does not matter.

The treasure and the pearl are sometimes preached as a transaction: give up enough and you will earn the kingdom. Both men sell everything because they have already found something worth more, and the first does it in his joy. Some preachers also reverse the parables, making Christ the merchant and the church the pearl; that reading has a long history and can be preached with care, but the text speaks of what a person finds and gives up. Avoid treating the mustard seed as a scientific claim to be defended or mocked, since its force lies in the proverbial smallness Galileans knew. Avoid the Scofield-style reading that makes leaven and birds sinister here, since Jesus says the kingdom is like leaven. And do not let verses 10 to 17 become a verdict on the Jewish people; those who do not see are defined by their response to Jesus, and the first disciples who do see are Jews.
teach.pastoral: The parables of separation and fire (verses 40 to 43 and 49 to 50) can frighten sensitive hearers, especially those prone to scrupulosity, who may wonder whether they are weeds. The parable's own logic helps: the servants cannot tell, the harvesters are angels, and the sorting is the Son of Man's, who sows good seed. Anxiety about whether one is wheat is not a sign of being a weed. The sower may press on parents and pastors grieving over people who received the word with joy and then fell away; the parable names that pain honestly and does not blame the sower. The Nazareth scene will reach anyone whose faith is dismissed by their own family, and Jesus knew that sorrow. And the treasure and the pearl may help those who have given up much for Christ, and feel only the loss, to remember the joy in which the giving began.

hard.q: Does Jesus speak in parables so that people will not understand and be healed?
hard.a:
The objection is strong even in Matthew's gentler form. Mark introduces Isaiah 6 with hina, ‘so that’, which makes concealment sound like the aim (Mark 4:12), and Matthew changes this to hoti, ‘because’: “This is why I speak to them in parables” (verse 13), because seeing they do not see. But the difficulty does not go away. Verse 11 still says the knowledge “has been given to you, but not to them”, verse 12 says that from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken, and verses 14 and 15 quote Isaiah in full, ending with the clause ‘otherwise they might see… and turn, and I would heal them’. Adolf Jülicher thought such a saying could not come from Jesus and assigned it to a church explaining Israel's unbelief; the literary critic Frank Kermode (The Genesis of Secrecy, 1979) took it as proof that stories shut outsiders out; Joel Marcus (The Mystery of the Kingdom of God, 1986) read the Markan form as real divine hardening within Jewish apocalyptic thought; and Calvin, in his Harmony of the Gospels (1555), read these verses of the just blinding of the reprobate. Jewish readers have rightly objected when Christian preaching turned ‘them’ into the Jewish people as such.

Responses begin with Matthew's own wording. John Chrysostom (Homily 45 on Matthew) stressed that the text says ‘seeing, they do not see’, so their blindness is self-chosen, and that Isaiah's words in verse 15 say that they themselves closed their eyes; if God did not wish them to hear, he argued, Jesus would simply have been silent, and parables are meant to rouse. Many modern commentators agree that Matthew's ‘because’ makes the parables a response to hardness already shown in chapters 11 and 12, not its cause, and that the principle of verse 12 describes how receiving light leads to more while refusing it leads to less. Others, in the Augustinian and Reformed tradition, hold that Matthew keeps both God's sovereign giving (verse 11) and human refusal (verse 15), as Isaiah did, and that the two are not rivals. Still others read Isaiah's words as the prophet's lament over the likely result of his preaching rather than its purpose. Christians who stress God's sovereign choice and those who stress human freedom have read these verses differently for centuries. The chapter itself ends each public section with an open call, “He who has ears, let him hear” (verses 9 and 43), and the disciples, no wiser than the crowd, are simply those who came and asked.

hard.q: Were the brothers and sisters of Jesus in verses 55 and 56 children of Mary and Joseph?
hard.a:
Christians have given three answers since the fourth century, and each deserves its strongest form. The first, named for Helvidius, who argued it at Rome before 383, holds that they were children of Joseph and Mary born after Jesus. Its case is the plain sense of adelphos and adelphē when used, as here, alongside mother and father; the phrases that Joseph ‘did not know her until’ she gave birth (1:25) and that Jesus was her ‘firstborn’ (Luke 2:7); and the way the brothers appear with Mary as a household (12:46). Helvidius appealed to Tertullian, and the Catholic scholar John P. Meier (A Marginal Jew, volume 1, 1991), setting aside later church teaching and judging as a historian, concluded that the most probable view is that they were full siblings. Most Protestants today hold this view, and skeptical historians generally assume it.

The second, named for Epiphanius of Salamis (Panarion 78, around 377), holds that they were children of Joseph by an earlier marriage. It appears already in the Protevangelium of James (second century), which presents Joseph as an older widower with sons, and it is the view of the Eastern Orthodox churches. Richard Bauckham (Jude and the Relatives of Jesus in the Early Church, 1990) has argued that it deserves more weight than it usually receives, while judging that the historical evidence cannot decide firmly between it and the Helvidian view. The third, named for Jerome (Against Helvidius, around 383), holds that they were cousins. Jerome noted that the Bible uses brother for wider kin (Genesis 13:8, 29:15), that Matthew later names a Mary as ‘the mother of James and Joseph’ at the cross (27:56), apparently not the mother of Jesus, and that Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple (John 19:26-27), which would be strange if she had other sons. Much Western Catholic teaching has followed Jerome. The Second Council of Constantinople (553) called Mary Ever-Virgin, and for Catholic and Orthodox Christians her perpetual virginity is settled teaching; Luther, Zwingli, and Calvin all continued to affirm it, while Calvin said that Matthew 1:25 tells us nothing either way about what happened afterward.

The question lies above the confessional floor. The creeds confess that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, which Matthew 1 teaches plainly and all three views affirm; they differ about Mary's later life and the meaning of a family word. Each view has an answer for the others' texts, and readers from each tradition can agree on what verses 55 and 56 are doing in Matthew: showing that Nazareth knew Jesus' family too well to believe he was more than one of them.

observe: What happens to the seed in each of the four kinds of ground, and how does Jesus explain each one in verses 19 to 23?
Why does the owner of the field refuse to let his servants pull up the weeds, and what does he say will happen at the harvest?
What do the people of Nazareth say about Jesus' family, and what does Matthew say about the miracles Jesus did there?
interpret: Matthew writes that Jesus speaks in parables because seeing they do not see (verse 13), where Mark writes ‘so that’. What difference does that change make, and what does verse 11 add?
Jesus says “The field is the world” (verse 38). Why have Christians argued over whether the parable also describes the church, and what follows from each reading?
What do the treasure and the pearl have in common, and what is different about how each man finds what he is looking for?
apply: Which of the worries, pressures, or attractions named in verses 21 and 22 most threatens to choke God's word in your life right now?
Where are you tempted to do the sorting that Jesus reserves for the harvest, in your church, your family, or your view of others?
The man with the treasure sold everything in his joy. What would it look like for your obedience to Jesus to be marked by that joy rather than by grim loss?
